To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), a representation designed around semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that are naturally understood by both humans and LLMs, enabling expressive, editable, and open-domain 3D generation without imposing restrictive geometric priors or expensive fine-tuning.
HPS inherits the flexibility of B-spline patches, while exposing an interface that leverages open-world capabilities of foundation models to reliably generate 3D. This paper introduces the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), an intermediate representation explicitly designed to bridge this gap. HPS represents objects as a rooted semantic tree over a collection of B-spline patches. A chair, for instance, is structured hierarchically into semantic components such as the seat, backrest, and legs, each a coherent cluster of smooth patches. By decoupling high-level structural organization from underlying coordinate instantiation, HPS provides a geometrically flexible, interpretable, and scalable interface that also enables controllable smoothness at a granular, patch-level resolution.

HPS parameterizes each patch using surface points rather than the abstract control-point lattices of classical spline formulations. This surface-point interface is a key design choice underlying HPS, as surface points correspond directly to visible geometry. The hierarchical semantic structure of HPS also enables intuitive and localized editing. Because semantic parts are explicitly mapped to geometric patch groups, edits can be targeted at arbitrary levels of granularity without regenerating the full object.

## Abstract

Pooling multi-site T1-weighted MRI increases power but introduces scanner-driven variability that can bias analyses. We propose a 3D patch-based conditional diffusion framework for MRI harmonization that preserves fine anatomical details while aligning image contrast across sites. Our method constructs site-invariant anatomical maps using gradient and high-frequency features, which guide patch-wise diffusion synthesis together with learnable site embeddings. Processing overlapping high-resolution patches avoids latent-decoder blurring and reduces memory requirements, enabling faithful preservation of fine anatomical detail. To further enhance anatomical fidelity, we employ manifold-constrained classifier-free guidance, stabilizing diffusion sampling while maintaining subject-specific structures. We evaluate our framework on a multi-site traveling-subject dataset and a clinically acquired pathological cohort, comparing against state-of-the-art harmonization methods. Results show that our approach effectively reduces site-related intensity variability, preserves anatomical and tissue-specific information, and maintains clinically relevant brain–cognition associations. These findings demonstrate that patch-based, anatomy-guided diffusion harmonization provides a robust, high-fidelity solution for multi-site MRI, with clear practical benefits for clinical datasets and downstream analyses. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11548607/)Abstract

Efficiently reconstructing complex and intricate surfaces at scale remains a significant challenge in 3D surface reconstruction. Recently, implicit neural representations have become a popular topic in 3D surface reconstruction. However, how to handle loop closure and bundle adjustment is a tricky problem for neural methods, because they learn the neural parameters globally. We present an algorithm that leverages the concept of surfels and expands relevant definitions to address such challenges. By integrating neural descriptors with surfels and framing surfel association as a deformation graph optimization problem, our method is able to effectively perform loop closure detection and loop correction in challenging scenarios. Furthermore, the surfel-level representation simplifies the complexity of 3D neural reconstruction. Meanwhile, the binding of neural descriptors to corresponding surfels produces a dense volumetric signed distance function (SDF), enabling the mesh reconstruction. The proposed representation is the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS). It is a tree of semantic labels (object, then part, then subpart) connected to groups of B-spline surface patches. A B-spline is a smooth, continuous surface representation. Here the LLM describes structured grids of surface points, and the system fits splines onto those points rather than asking the model for an abstract lattice of control points. Each patch has controls for smoothness or amplitude and for frequency: lower smoothness allows larger surface variation, and higher frequency makes the variation finer. Variation tapers at patch boundaries to help neighboring patches meet.
Generation runs as a loop. A generator writes executable code that creates the labeled surface points. The system fits and renders the patches from multiple views. A critic sees the renders alongside the prompt and, when applicable, a reference image, then gives a score and up to three actionable, part-specific fixes. The generator revises, and the highest-scoring version is kept.

The paper's ablation addresses this by comparing HPS with a point-cloud representation and with patches specified by B-spline control points. Critic iterations are disabled and the same in-context objects are used throughout. The test is on OmniObject3D with two open-source generator backbones, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Kimi K2.6. The metrics are FPD, a distribution-level point-cloud geometry-quality measure where lower is better, and Elo, which summarizes pairwise judgments by GPT-5.4-mini of structural coherence, detail quality, and surface appropriateness, where higher is better. Elo values are computed within each backbone column and cannot be compared across columns.
HPS wins in both columns. With Kimi K2.6 it reaches FPD 391 and Elo 1,206, against 745 and 930 for the control-point setting and 628 and 863 for the point-cloud setting.

The proposed representation is the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS). It is a tree of semantic labels (object, then part, then subpart) connected to groups of B-spline surface patches. A B-spline is a smooth, continuous surface representation. Here the LLM describes structured grids of surface points, and the system fits splines onto those points rather than asking the model for an abstract lattice of control points. Each patch has controls for smoothness or amplitude and for frequency: lower smoothness allows larger surface variation, and higher frequency makes the variation finer. Variation tapers at patch boundaries to help neighboring patches meet.
Generation runs as a loop. A generator writes executable code that creates the labeled surface points. The system fits and renders the patches from multiple views. A critic sees the renders alongside the prompt and, when applicable, a reference image, then gives a score and up to three actionable, part-specific fixes. The generator revises, and the highest-scoring version is kept.

The paper's ablation addresses this by comparing HPS with a point-cloud representation and with patches specified by B-spline control points. Critic iterations are disabled and the same in-context objects are used throughout. The test is on OmniObject3D with two open-source generator backbones, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Kimi K2.6. The metrics are FPD, a distribution-level point-cloud geometry-quality measure where lower is better, and Elo, which summarizes pairwise judgments by GPT-5.4-mini of structural coherence, detail quality, and surface appropriateness, where higher is better. Elo values are computed within each backbone column and cannot be compared across columns.
HPS wins in both columns. With Kimi K2.6 it reaches FPD 391 and Elo 1,206, against 745 and 930 for the control-point setting and 628 and 863 for the point-cloud setting.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising directions, yet extending their generative capabilities to 3D remains fundamentally challenging because existing 3D representations are not naturally compatible with language-based reasoning. Current approaches either depend on expensive fine-tuning or impose restrictive structural priors that sacrifice expressiveness and exclude organic shapes. We argue that the mismatch between LLM-native reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations is a core bottleneck of LLM-driven 3D generation. To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), a representation designed around semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that are naturally understood by both humans and LLMs, enabling expressive, editable, and open-domain 3D generation without imposing restrictive geometric priors or expensive fine-tuning.
Building upon HPS, we introduce SurfScaff3D, an interactive framework for text and image-to-3D generation. HPS inherits the flexibility of B-spline patches, while exposing an interface that leverages open-world capabilities of foundation models to reliably generate 3D. Its hierarchical part-level semantic labels enable targeted, natural-language edits at any level of granularity without re-running generation. Further, HPS offers explicit per-patch control over surface detail, enabling more expressive geometry capable of representing arbitrary objects. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art LLM-based 3D generation methods demonstrate strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.

## Methodology: Patch-Based Representation  
The core innovation lies in representing 3D shapes as collections of **Coons patches** - a subset of NURBS surfaces commonly used in CAD applications. A Coons patch is defined by four boundary cubic Bézier curves that share endpoints, inherently capturing the piecewise-smooth nature of man-made objects while allowing sharp edges at patch boundaries.  
*Figure 2: (a) A Coons patch defined by four boundary curves with control points. (b) Example of patch deformation. (c) Various geometric shapes represented as collections of Coons patches.*
### Template Construction  
Rather than manually designing patch layouts, the authors develop an algorithmic approach for creating category-specific templates:  
1. **Lattice Alignment**: Input cuboids (from segmented 3D models) are snapped to an integer lattice
2. **Face Splitting**: Faces are subdivided at grid coordinates
3. **Manifold Extraction**: Overlapping and interior faces are removed to ensure manifold topology
4. **Patch Simplification**: Adjacent quads are greedily merged to form larger, more meaningful patches  
This process automatically generates templates that capture the typical structure of objects within a category while maintaining geometric flexibility.
## Network Architecture and Training  
The system uses a ResNet-18 encoder to process input sketches, followed by fully connected layers that output control points for all Coons patches. The final layer weights are initialized to zero with biases set to template parameters, providing strong geometric priors.

## A Geometric View for Understanding Concept Learning and Neuron Interpretation in Sparse Autoencoders  
We propose a unified mathematical framework for a geometric understanding of concept learning and neuron interpretation in sparse autoencoders (SAEs). While SAEs improve interpretability of neural networks by learning sparse feature representations, a principled definition of ''concept'' and ''learning'' remains unclear. We formalize concepts as sets of data points and cast concept learning as a set-alignment problem between human-defined and model-induced concepts. This formulation distinguishes three increasingly strong notions of learning -- detection, separation, and approximation -- and yields geometric conditions, error bounds, and capacity constraints for when concepts can be represented by individual neurons or multi-neuron units. It also provides a set-theoretic account for common SAE phenomena, including feature splitting, feature absorption, feature families, and hierarchical concepts. Finally, we connect concept learning and neuron interpretation through formal concept analysis, showing that the two directions need not agree and that their many-to-many structure can be organized by concept lattices. Experiments on synthetic data with ReLU and Top-$K$ SAEs illustrate the theory and reveal the effects of SAE size and sparsity on concept learning.

Abstract
Current foundation models for 3D shapes excel at global tasks (retrieval, classification) but transfer poorly to local part-level reasoning. Recent approaches leverage vision and language foundation models to directly solve dense tasks through multi-view renderings and text queries. While promising, these pipelines require expensive inference over multiple renderings, depend heavily on large language-model (LLM) prompt engineering for captions, and fail to exploit the inherent 3D geometry of shapes. We address this gap by introducing an encoder-only 3D model that produces language-aligned patch-level features directly from point clouds. Our pre-training approach builds on existing data engines that generate part-annotated 3D shapes by pairing multi-view SAM regions with VLM captioning. Using this data, we train a point cloud transformer encoder in two stages: (1) distillation of dense 2D features from visual encoders such as DINOv2 into 3D patches, and (2) alignment of these patch embeddings with part-level text embeddings through a multi-positive contrastive objective. Our 3D encoder achieves zero-shot 3D part segmentation with fast single-pass inference without any test-time multi-view rendering, while significantly outperforming previous rendering-based and feed-forward approaches across several 3D part segmentation benchmarks.

octen.title: NeurIPS Poster ShapeCraft: LLM Agents for Structured, Textured and Interactive 3D Modeling
octen.snippet:
ShapeCraft: LLM Agents for Structured, Textured and Interactive 3D Modeling
Abstract
3D generation from natural language offers significant potential to reduce expert manual modeling efforts and enhance accessibility to 3D assets. However, existing methods often yield unstructured meshes and exhibit poor interactivity, making them impractical for artistic workflows. To address these limitations, we represent 3D assets as shape programs and introduce ShapeCraft, a novel multi-agent framework for text-to-3D generation. At its core, we propose a Graph-based Procedural Shape (GPS) representation that decomposes complex natural language into a structured graph of sub-tasks, thereby facilitating accurate LLM comprehension and interpretation of spatial relationships and semantic shape details. Specifically, LLM agents hierarchically parse user input to initialize GPS, then iteratively refine procedural modeling and painting to produce structured, textured, and interactive 3D assets. Qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate ShapeCraft's superior performance in generating geometrically accurate and semantically rich 3D assets compared to existing LLM-based agents. We further show the versatility of ShapeCraft through examples of animated and user-customized editing, highlighting its potential for broader interactive applications.

octen.title: ShapeScaffolder: Structure-Aware 3D Shape Generation from Text
octen.snippet:
Abstract
We present ShapeScaffolder, a structure-based neural network for generating colored 3D shapes based on text input. The approach, similar to providing scaffolds as internal structural supports and adding more details to them, aims to capture finer text-shape connections and improve the quality of generated shapes. Traditional text-to-shape methods often generate 3D shapes as a whole. However, humans tend to understand both shape and text as being structure-based. For example, a table is interpreted as being composed of legs, a seat, and a back; similarly, texts possess inherent linguistic structures that can be analyzed as dependency graphs, depicting the relationships between entities within the text. We believe structure-aware shape generation can bring finer text-shape connections and improve shape generation quality. However, the lack of explicit shape structure and the high freedom of text structure make cross-modality learning challenging. To address these challenges, we first build the structured shape implicit fields in an unsupervised manner. We then propose the part-level attention mechanism between shape parts and textual graph nodes to align the two modalities at the structural level. Finally, we employ a shape refiner to add further detail to the predicted structure, yielding the final results. Extensive experimentation demonstrates that our approaches outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of both shape fidelity and shape-text matching. Our methods also allow for part-level manipulation and improved part-level completeness.

octen.title: [2610.33484v3] Can One Hear Geometry? Gauge-Invariant Spectral Descriptors for Text-to-B-rep Retrieval
octen.snippet:
View PDF HTML (experimental)Abstract:Text-to-3D solid retrieval faces a fundamental representation gap: while natural language describes intrinsic shapes, Boundary Representation (B-rep) entangles precise geometry with arbitrary variations in pose, scale, and boundary encoding conventions. Existing methods either discretize B-reps at the cost of analytic precision, or learn features from topological graphs without explicit invariance guarantees. We propose **SpectraBRep** (*Spectral Geometry for Text-to-B-rep Retrieval*), a framework based on geometric invariance and spectral descriptors that mathematically eliminates representation ambiguities prior to cross-modal alignment. Formalizing translation, rotation, reflection, uniform scaling, and contour re-indexing via group actions, we exploit the planar-profile-and-extrusion structure of engineering solids to construct a unified spectral descriptor across cross-sectional regions, contour boundaries, and extrusion depths. On public benchmarks, our method achieves state-of-the-art recall performance across all evaluation metrics.

octen.title: PatchNets: Patch-Based Generalizable Deep Implicit 3D Shape   Representations
octen.snippet:
Implicit surface representations, such as signed-distance functions, combined
with deep learning have led to impressive models which can represent detailed
shapes of objects with arbitrary topology. Since a continuous function is
learned, the reconstructions can also be extracted at any arbitrary resolution.
However, large datasets such as ShapeNet are required to train such models. In
this paper, we present a new mid-level patch-based surface representation. At
the level of patches, objects across different categories share similarities,
which leads to more generalizable models. We then introduce a novel method to
learn this patch-based representation in a canonical space, such that it is as
object-agnostic as possible. We show that our representation trained on one
category of objects from ShapeNet can also well represent detailed shapes from
any other category. In addition, it can be trained using much fewer shapes,
compared to existing approaches. We show several applications of our new
representation, including shape interpolation and partial point cloud
completion. Due to explicit control over positions, orientations and scales of
patches, our representation is also more controllable compared to object-level
representations, which enables us to deform encoded shapes non-rigidly. cs.CV, cs.GR E. Tretschk, A. Tewari, Vladislav Golyanik, M. Zollhöfer, C. Stoll, Christian Theobalt

Abstract

Applying Gaussian Splatting to perception tasks for 3D scene understanding is becoming increasingly popular. Most existing works primarily focus on rendering 2D feature maps from novel viewpoints, which leads to an imprecise 3D language field with outlier languages, ultimately failing to align objects in 3D space. To this end, we propose a Language-Embedded Surface Field (LangSurf), which accurately aligns the 3D language fields with the surface of objects, facilitating precise 2D and 3D segmentation with text query, widely expanding the downstream tasks such as removal and editing. In addition, we also introduce the Hierarchical-Context Awareness Module to extract features at the image level for contextual information then perform hierarchical mask pooling using masks segmented by SAM to obtain fine-grained language features in different hierarchies. Extensive experiments on open-vocabulary 2D and 3D semantic segmentation demonstrate that LangSurf outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method LangSplat by a large margin. parallel.snippet:
This paper introduces the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold
(HPS) , an intermediate representation explicitly designed to bridge this gap. HPS represents objects as a rooted se- mantic tree over a collection of B-spline patches. A chair, for instance, is structured hierarchically into semantic com- ponents such as the seat, backrest, and legs, each a coherent cluster of smooth patches. By decoupling high-level struc- tural organization from underlying coordinate instantiation, HPS provides a geometrically flexible, interpretable, and scalable interface that also enables controllable smoothness at a granular, patch-level resolution. HPS parameterizes each patch using surface points rather than the abstract control-point lattices of classical spline formulations. This surface-point interface is a key design choice underlying HPS, as surface points correspond directly to visible geometry. Similar observations were made by [36] in the related domain of sketch generation, and our ablations (Table 5) further show that surface-point parameterization is more intuitive for LLMs than direct control-point prediction, as it better aligns with the geomet- ric concepts expressed in natural language. The hierarchical semantic structure of HPS also enables intuitive and local- ized editing. Because semantic parts are explicitly mapped to geometric patch groups, edits can be targeted at arbitrary levels of granularity without regenerating the full object. Building upon HPS, we introduce SurfScaff3D (short for Surface Scaffold in 3D), a training-free 3D generation framework that enables programmatic construction of sur- face geometry that can be rendered into views for direct in- spection of local geometry. parallel.snippet:
The proposed representation is the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS). [p2] It is a tree of semantic labels (object, then part, then subpart) connected to groups of B-spline surface patches. [p5] A B-spline is a smooth, continuous surface representation. Here the LLM describes structured grids of surface points, and the system fits splines onto those points rather than asking the model for an abstract lattice of control points. [p5] Each patch has controls for smoothness or amplitude and for frequency: lower smoothness allows larger surface variation, and higher frequency makes the variation finer. Variation tapers at patch boundaries to help neighboring patches meet. [p5]
Generation runs as a loop. A generator writes executable code that creates the labeled surface points. The system fits and renders the patches from multiple views. A critic sees the renders alongside the prompt and, when applicable, a reference image, then gives a score and up to three actionable, part-specific fixes. The generator revises, and the highest-scoring version is kept. [p6] [p6] The authors describe the method as training-free, though it still relies on model calls.

parallel.snippet:
高品質な3Dオブジェクトの制作には、今なお専門的なツールと多大な手作業が必要です。 [p2] LLMベースの代替手法では、モデルが生成しやすい表現を使うために、形状の柔軟性を犠牲にする傾向がありました。 [p2] 著者らはこれを、単により強力なモデルを選べばよいという問題ではなく、言語モデルの推論と、モデルに指定を求める幾何形状との不一致だと捉えています。
従来の2つの手法が、このトレードオフを示しています。NURBGenは、テキストからCADを生成するため、制御点を含む構造化されたNURBSパラメーターを出力するようにLLMをファインチューニングしており、その設定はCAD学習データに結び付いています（ NURBGen論文 ）。Articraftは既製のLLMを使い、関節構造を持つオブジェクト向けのドメイン固有SDKを操作するコードを記述します。このSDKのインターフェースには、あらかじめ定義された幾何形状とモデリング操作が含まれています（ Articraft論文 ）。SurfScaff3Dは、連続したスプラインパッチにグループ化された、ラベル付きの表面点を公開します。モデルは制御点の格子を直接予測することなく多様な表面を構築でき、固定された基本形状の語彙にも制限されません。ここまでの説明は背景です。この違いを検証するのは、論文独自の実験です。

 名前付き表面と閉ループ生成

提案する表現は、階層パッチ・スキャフォールド（HPS）です。 [p2] これは、意味ラベル（オブジェクト、パーツ、サブパーツの順）からなる木構造を、Bスプライン表面パッチのグループに結び付けたものです。 [p5] Bスプラインは、滑らかで連続した表面表現です。ここではLLMが構造化された表面点の格子を記述し、モデルに抽象的な制御点格子を求めるのではなく、システムがその点にスプラインを当てはめます。 [p5] 各パッチには、滑らかさまたは振幅、および周波数を調節する制御機能があります。滑らかさを低くすると表面の変化が大きくなり、周波数を高くすると変化が細かくなります。パッチ境界では変化を弱め、隣接するパッチが接続しやすくします。 [p5]
生成はループとして実行されます。生成器が、ラベル付きの表面点を作成する実行可能コードを記述します。システムは複数の視点からパッチを当てはめてレンダリングします。批評器は、プロンプトと、該当する場合は参照画像とともにレンダリング結果を確認し、スコアと最大3つの具体的なパーツ別修正案を提示します。生成器が修正を加え、最も高いスコアのバージョンが保持されます。 [p6] [p6] 著者らはこの手法を学習不要と説明していますが、モデル呼び出しには依存しています。
SurfScaff3Dの概要図。生成器、レンダリング、批評器のフィードバック、ジェット機のパーツ階層、表面制御の例を示しています パイプライン：左側に生成コードと表面レンダリング、右側に批評器のフィードバック、中央にジェット機の名前付き階層（エンジン、翼、ナセル、ファン、ブレード）を示します。制御図は周波数と振幅を表面の見た目に対応付け、パイナップル、ベッドフレーム、リンゴ、木製フルートなどの例を示しています。 [p5]

 スキャフォールド自体に効果はあるのでしょうか？

性能が基盤モデルと反復的な改良ループだけを反映しているのではないか、というのは自然な疑問です。論文のアブレーションでは、HPSを点群表現およびBスプライン制御点で指定したパッチと比較し、この点に対処しています。批評器による反復は無効にし、同じインコンテキストオブジェクトを全条件で使用しています。テストにはOmniObject3Dと、2つのオープンソース生成バックボーンであるQwen3.6-35B-A3BおよびKimi K2.6を用いています。指標はFPDとEloです。FPDは点群の幾何品質を分布レベルで測る指標で、値が低いほど優れています。Eloは、構造的一貫性、ディテールの品質、表面の適切さに関するGPT-5.4-miniのペアワイズ判定を集約したもので、値が高いほど優れています。Elo値は各バックボーンの列内で算出されており、列をまたいで比較することはできません。 [p8]

Two prior approaches illustrate the trade. NURBGen fine-tunes an LLM to emit structured NURBS parameters, including control points, for text-to-CAD, and its setup is tied to CAD training data ( NURBGen paper ). Articraft uses an off-the-shelf LLM to write code against a domain-specific SDK for articulated objects, whose interface includes predefined geometry and modeling operations ( Articraft paper ). SurfScaff3D exposes labeled surface points grouped into continuous spline patches. The model can build varied surfaces without predicting a control-point lattice directly and without being confined to a fixed primitive vocabulary. This is background; the paper's own experiments are what test the difference.

 Named surfaces, closed-loop generation

The proposed representation is the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS). [p2] It is a tree of semantic labels (object, then part, then subpart) connected to groups of B-spline surface patches. [p5] A B-spline is a smooth, continuous surface representation. Here the LLM describes structured grids of surface points, and the system fits splines onto those points rather than asking the model for an abstract lattice of control points. [p5] Each patch has controls for smoothness or amplitude and for frequency: lower smoothness allows larger surface variation, and higher frequency makes the variation finer. Variation tapers at patch boundaries to help neighboring patches meet. [p5]
Generation runs as a loop. A generator writes executable code that creates the labeled surface points. The system fits and renders the patches from multiple views. A critic sees the renders alongside the prompt and, when applicable, a reference image, then gives a score and up to three actionable, part-specific fixes. The generator revises, and the highest-scoring version is kept. [p6] [p6] The authors describe the method as training-free, though it still relies on model calls.

Current approaches either depend on expensive fine-tuning or impose restrictive structural priors that sacrifice expressiveness and exclude organic shapes. We argue that the mismatch between LLM-native reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations is a core bottleneck of LLM-driven 3D generation. To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), a representation designed around semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that are naturally understood by both humans and LLMs, enabling expressive, editable, and open-domain 3D generation without imposing restrictive geometric priors or expensive fine-tuning. Building upon HPS, we introduce SurfScaff3D, an interactive framework for text and image-to-3D generation. HPS inherits the flexibility of B-spline patches, while exposing an interface that leverages open-world capabilities of foundation models to reliably generate 3D. Its hierarchical part-level semantic labels enable targeted, natural-language edits at any level of granularity without re-running generation. Further, HPS offers explicit per-patch control over surface detail, enabling more expressive geometry capable of representing arbitrary objects. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art LLM-based 3D generation methods demonstrate strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.

parallel-fast.title: SurfScaff3D：LLMベースの3Dオブジェクト生成に向けた幾何表現と意味表現の橋渡し | alphaXiv
parallel-fast.snippet:
コピー
3Dの時計があり、モデリングソフトを開いたり最初から作り直したりせずに、ストラップを別のものにしたり、ベゼルを厚くしたりしたいと想像してください。SurfScaff3Dの著者らは、まさにこのような一連の編集を示しています。自然言語の指示に従って生成済みの時計を段階的に変更し、変更されたパッチをハイライト表示します。彼らの工夫は、柔軟な表面からなるオブジェクトを名前付きパーツとして表現することです。これにより、言語モデルは限られた固定形状のメニューから選ぶのではなく、パーツ名を指定して操作できます。
プロジェクトページで 対話型の時計編集手順 を試せます。これは動画ではなく対話型ビューアーです。生成された時計を4段階で編集でき、編集前後を切り替えて表示できるほか、各段階で変更されたパッチがオレンジ色でハイライト表示されます。

 この論文が取り組む課題

高品質な3Dオブジェクトの制作には、今なお専門的なツールと多大な手作業が必要です。 [p2] LLMベースの代替手法では、モデルが生成しやすい表現を使うために、形状の柔軟性を犠牲にする傾向がありました。 [p2] 著者らはこれを、単により強力なモデルを選べばよいという問題ではなく、言語モデルの推論と、モデルに指定を求める幾何形状との不一致だと捉えています。
従来の2つの手法が、このトレードオフを示しています。NURBGenは、テキストからCADを生成するため、制御点を含む構造化されたNURBSパラメーターを出力するようにLLMをファインチューニングしており、その設定はCAD学習データに結び付いています（ NURBGen論文 ）。Articraftは既製のLLMを使い、関節構造を持つオブジェクト向けのドメイン固有SDKを操作するコードを記述します。このSDKのインターフェースには、あらかじめ定義された幾何形状とモデリング操作が含まれています（ Articraft論文 ）。SurfScaff3Dは、連続したスプラインパッチにグループ化された、ラベル付きの表面点を公開します。モデルは制御点の格子を直接予測することなく多様な表面を構築でき、固定された基本形状の語彙にも制限されません。ここまでの説明は背景です。この違いを検証するのは、論文独自の実験です。

 名前付き表面と閉ループ生成

提案する表現は、階層パッチ・スキャフォールド（HPS）です。 [p2] これは、意味ラベル（オブジェクト、パーツ、サブパーツの順）からなる木構造を、Bスプライン表面パッチのグループに結び付けたものです。 [p5] Bスプラインは、滑らかで連続した表面表現です。ここではLLMが構造化された表面点の格子を記述し、モデルに抽象的な制御点格子を求めるのではなく、システムがその点にスプラインを当てはめます。 [p5] 各パッチには、滑らかさまたは振幅、および周波数を調節する制御機能があります。滑らかさを低くすると表面の変化が大きくなり、周波数を高くすると変化が細かくなります。パッチ境界では変化を弱め、隣接するパッチが接続しやすくします。 [p5]
生成はループとして実行されます。生成器が、ラベル付きの表面点を作成する実行可能コードを記述します。システムは複数の視点からパッチを当てはめてレンダリングします。批評器は、プロンプトと、該当する場合は参照画像とともにレンダリング結果を確認し、スコアと最大3つの具体的なパーツ別修正案を提示します。生成器が修正を加え、最も高いスコアのバージョンが保持されます。 [p6] [p6] 著者らはこの手法を学習不要と説明していますが、モデル呼び出しには依存しています。
SurfScaff3Dの概要図。生成器、レンダリング、批評器のフィードバック、ジェット機のパーツ階層、表面制御の例を示しています パイプライン：左側に生成コードと表面レンダリング、右側に批評器のフィードバック、中央にジェット機の名前付き階層（エンジン、翼、ナセル、ファン、ブレード）を示します。制御図は周波数と振幅を表面の見た目に対応付け、パイナップル、ベッドフレーム、リンゴ、木製フルートなどの例を示しています。 [p5]

 スキャフォールド自体に効果はあるのでしょうか？

性能が基盤モデルと反復的な改良ループだけを反映しているのではないか、というのは自然な疑問です。論文のアブレーションでは、HPSを点群表現およびBスプライン制御点で指定したパッチと比較し、この点に対処しています。批評器による反復は無効にし、同じインコンテキストオブジェクトを全条件で使用しています。テストにはOmniObject3Dと、2つのオープンソース生成バックボーンであるQwen3.6-35B-A3BおよびKimi K2.6を用いています

## A Curve Is a Hypothesis, Not Yet an Explanation

The previous article showed that concepts can form circles, simplices, and other multi-dimensional structures. It is tempting to run PCA, see a curve, and declare that the model has learned a manifold. That conclusion moves too quickly.

A projection can bend or separate points even when the high-dimensional organization is different. Prompt templates can introduce nuisance variation. A smooth color gradient can appear because the labels were used to choose the projection. Most importantly, a representation can correlate with a variable without being used by the model.

Suppose activations for ages from 10 to 100 trace a loop in a three-dimensional plot. A useful analysis must answer at least four questions:

1. Is the apparent structure low-dimensional in the original activation space?
1. Does it generalize to prompts that were not used to fit it?
1. Do positions along it correspond consistently to age rather than a prompt artifact?
1. Does changing the representation along the structure change the model's computation as predicted?

The object we are trying to establish is therefore stronger than a visualization.

This paper introduces the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), an intermediate representation explicitly designed to bridge this gap. HPS represents objects as a rooted semantic tree over a collection of B-spline patches. A chair, for instance, is structured hierarchically into semantic components such as the seat, backrest, and legs, each a coherent cluster of smooth patches. By decoupling high-level structural organization from underlying coordinate instantiation, HPS provides a geometrically flexible, interpretable, and scalable interface that also enables controllable smoothness at a granular, patch-level resolution.

This surface-point interface is a key design choice underlying HPS, as surface points correspond directly to visible geometry. ultimate.snippet:
The proposed representation is the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS). It is a tree of semantic labels (object, then part, then subpart) connected to groups of B-spline surface patches. A B-spline is a smooth, continuous surface representation. Here the LLM describes structured grids of surface points, and the system fits splines onto those points rather than asking the model for an abstract lattice of control points. Each patch has controls for smoothness or amplitude and for frequency: lower smoothness allows larger surface variation, and higher frequency makes the variation finer. Variation tapers at patch boundaries to help neighboring patches meet.
Generation runs as a loop. A generator writes executable code that creates the labeled surface points. The system fits and renders the patches from multiple views. A critic sees the renders alongside the prompt and, when applicable, a reference image, then gives a score and up to three actionable, part-specific fixes. The generator revises, and the highest-scoring version is kept.

The paper's ablation addresses this by comparing HPS with a point-cloud representation and with patches specified by B-spline control points. Critic iterations are disabled and the same in-context objects are used throughout. The test is on OmniObject3D with two open-source generator backbones, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Kimi K2.6. The metrics are FPD, a distribution-level point-cloud geometry-quality measure where lower is better, and Elo, which summarizes pairwise judgments by GPT-5.4-mini of structural coherence, detail quality, and surface appropriateness, where higher is better. Elo values are computed within each backbone column and cannot be compared across columns.
HPS wins in both columns. With Kimi K2.6 it reaches FPD 391 and Elo 1,206, against 745 and 930 for the control-point setting and 628 and 863 for the point-cloud setting.

ultimate.title: SurfScaff3D : Bridging Geometric and Semantic Representations for LLM-based 3D Object Generation
ultimate.snippet:
Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising directions, yet extending their generative capabilities to 3D remains fundamentally challenging because existing 3D representations are not naturally compatible with language-based reasoning. Current approaches either depend on expensive fine-tuning or impose restrictive structural priors that sacrifice expressiveness and exclude organic shapes. We argue that the mismatch between LLM-native reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations is a core bottleneck of LLM-driven 3D generation. To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), a representation designed around semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that are naturally understood by both humans and LLMs, enabling expressive, editable, and open-domain 3D generation without imposing restrictive geometric priors or expensive fine-tuning.
Building upon HPS, we introduce SurfScaff3D, an interactive framework for text and image-to-3D generation. HPS inherits the flexibility of B-spline patches, while exposing an interface that leverages open-world capabilities of foundation models to reliably generate 3D. Its hierarchical part-level semantic labels enable targeted, natural-language edits at any level of granularity without re-running generation. Further, HPS offers explicit per-patch control over surface detail, enabling more expressive geometry capable of representing arbitrary objects. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art LLM-based 3D generation methods demonstrate strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.
